sources.title: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1426 on type-approval of automated driving systems
sources.topic: EU law – type approval
sources.summary: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1426 lays down uniform procedures and technical specifications for type-approval of the automated driving system of fully automated vehicles under Regulation (EU) 2019/2144. It defines the principal EU technical-assessment framework for ADS safety, documentation, testing and approval.
sources.why_it_matters: It is the central EU instrument for demonstrating ADS compliance at type approval and therefore a primary benchmark for safety evidence before automated-vehicle deployment.
sources.keywords: EU law – type approval; Type Approval; automated vehicles
sources.citation: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1426 of 5 August 2022, OJ L 221, 26.8.2022, pp. 1–64.

sources.title: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/481 amending Regulation (EU) 2022/1426
sources.topic: Automated parking systems and ADS type approval
sources.summary: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/481 amends the EU ADS type-approval framework in Regulation (EU) 2022/1426. It removes the earlier limitation on the number of registrations for automated parking systems, enabling those systems to be approved and deployed in unlimited series under the EU framework.
sources.why_it_matters: The amendment demonstrates the transition from restricted automated-vehicle approvals toward broader market deployment and shows how the EU ADS framework is being adapted as applications mature.
sources.keywords: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/481; CELEX 32026R0481; automated parking systems; automated valet parking; ADS; fully automated vehicles; unlimited series; type approval; Regulation (EU) 2022/1426; Regulation (EU) 2019/2144
sources.citation: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/481 of 3 March 2026, OJ L, 2026/481, 4.3.2026.

sources.title: Council Decision (EU) 2026/1411 on the EU position at the 199th session of UNECE WP.29
sources.topic: UNECE WP.29 and Automated Driving Systems
sources.summary: Council Decision (EU) 2026/1411 establishes the position to be taken on behalf of the European Union at the 199th session of UNECE WP.29. Its Annex covers working documents for new automated-driving regulatory instruments and links EU vehicle-safety policy with the adoption of harmonised UNECE ADS requirements.
sources.why_it_matters: The Decision provides the formal EU position supporting new UNECE ADS instruments and shows how international vehicle regulation feeds into the EU type-approval framework.
sources.keywords: Council Decision (EU) 2026/1411; UNECE WP.29; ADS; automated driving systems; type approval; UN Regulation; UN GTR; ECE/TRANS/WP.29/2026/137; ECE/TRANS/WP.29/2026/139
sources.citation: Council Decision (EU) 2026/1411 of 22 June 2026, OJ L, 2026/1411, 23.6.2026.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2018/858 on the approval and market surveillance of motor vehicles
sources.topic: EU law – type approval
sources.summary: Regulation (EU) 2018/858 establishes the EU framework for approval and market surveillance of motor vehicles, trailers, systems, components and separate technical units. It supplies the general type-approval architecture within which automated-vehicle safety requirements and implementing measures are integrated and recognised across the Union.
sources.why_it_matters: It provides the horizontal EU type-approval framework that determines how automated-vehicle technical requirements are assessed, approved, monitored and placed on the EU market.
sources.keywords: EU law – type approval; Type Approval; automated vehicles
sources.citation: Regulation (EU) 2018/858 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 May 2018, OJ L 151, 14.6.2018, pp. 1–218.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 on type-approval requirements for motor vehicles and general safety
sources.topic: EU law – type approval
sources.summary: Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 establishes EU type-approval requirements for vehicle general safety and protection of occupants and vulnerable road users. It provides the legislative basis for detailed EU technical measures concerning automated and fully automated vehicles, including the implementing framework for automated driving systems.
sources.why_it_matters: The Regulation is the legislative gateway connecting general EU vehicle-safety law with detailed ADS type-approval rules and deployment of fully automated vehicles.
sources.keywords: EU law – type approval; Safety; automated vehicles
sources.citation: Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2019, OJ L 325, 16.12.2019, pp. 1–40.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 on type-approval requirements for motor vehicles and general safety
sources.topic: EU law
sources.summary: Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 establishes EU type-approval requirements for vehicle general safety and the protection of occupants and vulnerable road users. It provides the legislative basis for EU technical measures addressing automated and fully automated vehicles, including the implementing framework for automated driving systems.
sources.why_it_matters: The Regulation is the legislative gateway connecting general EU vehicle safety law with detailed ADS type-approval rules and the deployment of fully automated vehicles.
sources.keywords: EU law
sources.citation: Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2019, OJ L 325, 16.12.2019, pp. 1–40.

sources.title: International Convention relative to Motor Traffic (Paris, 24 April 1926)
sources.topic: History of mobility regulation – international motor-traffic harmonisation and approved type
sources.summary: The 1926 International Convention relative to Motor Traffic was an early multilateral instrument coordinating road-traffic rules and cross-border motor-vehicle movement. It forms part of the historical development of international road-traffic law that later led to the Geneva and Vienna convention frameworks.
sources.why_it_matters: The Convention shows that cross-border mobility eventually required international legal harmonisation, providing a historical parallel to current efforts to harmonise automated-driving regulation and evidence.
sources.keywords: international motor traffic; 1926 Paris Convention; approved type; vehicle examination; driver authorisation; national traffic law; road signs; type approval genealogy
sources.citation: International Convention relative to Motor Traffic, Paris, 24 April 1926, Treaty Series No. 11 (1930).

sources.title: Vienna Convention on Road Traffic – 2021 amendment to Article 1 and new Article 34 bis
sources.topic: International law
sources.summary: United Nations depositary notification for the 2021 amendment to the Vienna Convention on Road Traffic, adding definitions relevant to automated driving systems and a new Article 34 bis. The amendment adapts the Convention’s road-traffic framework to automated driving while preserving the Convention as the governing international legal instrument.
sources.why_it_matters: The amendment is a core international-law bridge between automated-driving technology and road-traffic rules, clarifying how automated driving can operate within the Vienna Convention framework.
sources.keywords: International law; Safety; automated vehicles
sources.citation: United Nations, C.N.5.2021.Reissued.15012021.TREATIES-XI.B.19, Amendment to Article 1 and new Article 34 bis of the Convention on Road Traffic, 14 January 2021.

sources.title: Vienna Convention on Road Traffic – amendment to Article 8(5 bis)
sources.topic: International law
sources.summary: The 2014 amendment to the Vienna Convention on Road Traffic added Article 8(5 bis), allowing vehicle systems that influence how vehicles are driven to be deemed compatible with the Convention when they conform to applicable international vehicle regulations or can be overridden or switched off by the driver.
sources.why_it_matters: This amendment created an early international-law accommodation for vehicle automation and illustrates how road-traffic law began adapting before comprehensive automated-driving frameworks emerged.
sources.keywords: International law; Safety; automated vehicles
sources.citation: UNECE Working Party on Road Traffic Safety, ECE/TRANS/WP.1/145, amendment to Article 8(5 bis) of the 1968 Convention on Road Traffic, adopted 26 March 2014.

sources.title: Act No. 106/2018 Coll. on the Operation of Vehicles in Road Traffic (Zákon č. 106/2018 Z. z.)
sources.topic: Vehicle approval and test-operation framework for automated vehicles
sources.summary: Act No. 106/2018 Coll. regulates technical requirements, vehicle approval, market surveillance and conditions for road operation in Slovakia. Section 49 provides the national permit pathway for test operation of automated and fully automated vehicles, including safety evidence, operating conditions, route or time restrictions, data and insurance requirements.
sources.why_it_matters: It is the principal Slovak vehicle-law basis for public-road testing of automated vehicles and therefore defines the national authorisation layer before broader commercial deployment.
sources.keywords: Slovakia; Act 106/2018; § 49; automated vehicle; fully automated vehicle; test operation; permit; safety evidence; PZP; route; type approval
sources.citation: Zákon č. 106/2018 Z. z. o prevádzke vozidiel v cestnej premávke a o zmene a doplnení niektorých zákonov.

sources.title: Act No. 131/2026 Coll. amending the Slovak Road Traffic Act and related legislation (Zákon č. 131/2026 Z. z.)
sources.topic: Test operation – pre-series vehicles and procedural amendment of § 49 Act No. 106/2018 Coll.
sources.summary: Slovak Act No. 131/2026 Coll. amends the Road Traffic Act and related legislation, including provisions relevant to automated mobility and test operation. The Act was adopted on 2 June 2026, promulgated on 18 June 2026 and contains provisions effective from 1 September 2026.
sources.why_it_matters: The Act updates the current Slovak operational and testing framework for automated vehicles and is therefore essential for interpreting the national law applicable from September 2026.
sources.keywords: Slovakia; Act 106/2018; § 49; test operation; pre-series vehicle; automated vehicle; trial permit; 1 September 2026; regulatory normalisation
sources.citation: Zákon č. 131/2026 Z. z., ktorým sa mení a dopĺňa zákon č. 8/2009 Z. z. o cestnej premávke a ktorým sa menia a dopĺňajú niektoré zákony.

sources.title: Act No. 429/2022 Coll. amending laws in connection with the development of automated vehicles (Zákon č. 429/2022 Z. z.)
sources.topic: National legislation
sources.summary: Slovak Act No. 429/2022 Coll. amended several statutes in connection with the development of automated vehicles. It introduced and adjusted national legal concepts supporting automated-vehicle testing and operation, forming an important legislative step in Slovakia’s transition from conventional road-traffic regulation toward automated mobility.
sources.why_it_matters: The Act is a foundational Slovak legislative package for automated mobility and explains the national legal basis on which later testing, operational and institutional rules build.
sources.keywords: National legislation; Testing; automated vehicles
sources.citation: Zákon č. 429/2022 Z. z., ktorým sa menia a dopĺňajú niektoré zákony v súvislosti s rozvojom automatizovaných vozidiel.

sources.title: Act No. 8/2009 Coll. on Road Traffic (Zákon č. 8/2009 Z. z. o cestnej premávke)
sources.topic: Road-traffic rules relevant to automated and fully automated vehicles
sources.summary: Slovakia’s Road Traffic Act regulates road-traffic rules, rights and duties of road users, vehicle driving, public-administration competences, vehicle registration and offences. Its current framework also contains selected rules relevant to automated mobility, including human supervision, takeover duties and specific treatment of automated delivery vehicles.
sources.why_it_matters: It is the primary Slovak source for the traffic-law obligations that automated vehicles and their human or organisational actors must satisfy during testing and deployment.
sources.keywords: Slovakia; road traffic; automated driving; supervision; automated delivery vehicle; § 55b; driver; remote takeover; behavioural rules
sources.citation: Zákon č. 8/2009 Z. z. o cestnej premávke a o zmene a doplnení niektorých zákonov.

sources.title: Automated road freight transport systems - France
sources.topic: France - automated road freight transport systems
sources.summary: 2024 French decree extending the automated road transport system safety and governance framework to automated freight.
sources.why_it_matters: Broadens the French comparator beyond passenger transport and strengthens the system/service character of post-type-approval deployment governance.
sources.keywords: France; automated freight; automated road transport system; goods transport; safety demonstration; remote intervention; service organiser; operator; Regulation EU 2022/1426
sources.citation: France, Décret n° 2024-1063 du 25 novembre 2024 relatif au transport routier automatisé de marchandises, JORF 27 November 2024.

sources.title: Automated Vehicles Act 2024
sources.topic: Automated mobility
sources.summary: The United Kingdom’s Automated Vehicles Act 2024 creates the statutory framework for authorising self-driving vehicles and regulating their use on roads and other public places. It establishes concepts and institutional responsibilities for authorised automated use, safety assessment, operator accountability, monitoring and automated passenger services.
sources.why_it_matters: The Act is a major national deployment model that separates vehicle authorisation, responsible actors and service regulation, offering a comparator for EU and Slovak frameworks.
sources.keywords: automated mobility
sources.citation: Automated Vehicles Act 2024, 2024 c. 10.

sources.title: Croatia – amendments to the Road Traffic Safety Act introducing fully automated vehicles
sources.topic: Fully automated vehicles – road operation, actors, traffic offences and data duties
sources.summary: Croatian legislative amendments introduce a legal basis for fully automated vehicles within the national road-traffic framework. The measure supports the transition from testing toward regulated operation and provides national rules relevant to vehicle use, responsible actors and interaction with the wider road-traffic system.
sources.why_it_matters: Croatia is an important EU comparator for national deployment law because it combines EU vehicle-approval rules with domestic operational requirements for fully automated vehicles.
sources.keywords: Croatia; fully automated vehicle; road traffic; operating area; remote intervention; owner liability; traffic offences; event data; video surveillance; automated driving; deployment
sources.citation: Croatia, Zakon o izmjenama i dopunama Zakona o sigurnosti prometa na cestama, NN 145/2024.

sources.title: Croatia – amendments to the Road Transport Act on fully automated passenger transport
sources.topic: Fully automated passenger transport – statutory basis for service-testing procedure
sources.summary: Croatian amendments to the Road Transport Act adapt passenger-transport regulation to fully automated vehicles. The legislation connects automated driving with transport-service rules and therefore addresses the layer beyond vehicle technical approval, including the legal conditions under which automated passenger services can be integrated into the national transport system.
sources.why_it_matters: The amendments show how automated passenger services require transport-law rules in addition to vehicle approval and road-traffic law, making Croatia a useful deployment comparator.
sources.keywords: Croatia; road transport; fully automated passenger transport; service testing; ministerial regulation; public passenger transport; deployment assurance; 2026
sources.citation: Croatia, Zakon o izmjenama i dopunama Zakona o prijevozu u cestovnom prometu, NN 77/2026.

sources.title: Croatia – special conditions and real-world service testing for fully automated vehicles
sources.topic: Pre-deployment service validation of fully automated passenger transport
sources.summary: Croatian implementing rules set special conditions for testing and operating services with fully automated vehicles in real traffic. They complement the statutory framework by specifying operational requirements for controlled real-world use and provide evidence on how an EU Member State structures the transition from testing to service deployment.
sources.why_it_matters: The rules provide a practical national model for translating automated-vehicle legislation into conditions for real-world testing and service operation within an EU Member State.
sources.keywords: Croatia; fully automated passenger transport; real-world testing; registered sample vehicle; remote intervention operator; incident management; MRM; cybersecurity; service validation; commission; deployment assurance
sources.citation: Croatia, Pravilnik o izmjenama i dopunama Pravilnika o posebnim uvjetima za vozila kojima se obavlja javni cestovni prijevoz i prijevoz za vlastite potrebe, NN 154/2024, arts 13a–13d.

sources.title: Decree No. 2021-873 of 29 June 2021 implementing Ordonnance No. 2021-443 (Décret n° 2021-873)
sources.topic: France - safety demonstration and mise-en-service regime for automated road transport systems
sources.summary: French Decree No. 2021-873 implements the 2021 legal framework for vehicles with delegated driving. It supplies detailed regulatory provisions needed to operationalise the Ordonnance and complements the Road Code rules governing automated-driving conditions, system use and the allocation of responsibilities in real-world operation.
sources.why_it_matters: The Decree demonstrates how high-level automated-driving legislation is converted into detailed operational requirements and provides a useful comparator for implementing national deployment rules.
sources.keywords: France; STRA; automated road transport system; safety case; mise en service; qualified body; service organiser; operator; remote intervention; predefined route; safety management
sources.citation: France, Decret 2021-873 du 29 juin 2021 implementing Ordonnance 2021-443, Journal officiel, 30 June 2021.

sources.title: French Road Code – Chapter 9: Provisions applicable to vehicles with delegated driving (Code de la route, articles L319-1 to L319-4)
sources.topic: Automated mobility
sources.summary: Chapter 9 of the French Road Code contains provisions applicable to vehicles with delegated driving, including conditions of use for automated driving systems and related information and operational requirements. The provisions were introduced through the 2021 French legislative framework for delegated-driving vehicles.
sources.why_it_matters: The provisions show how France integrates automated-driving use conditions into ordinary road law and provide a national comparator for operational duties after vehicle approval.
sources.keywords: automated mobility
sources.citation: Code de la route, chapitre 9, articles L319-1 à L319-4, créés par l’ordonnance n° 2021-443 du 14 avril 2021.

sources.title: German Road Traffic Act (StVG) § 1a – Motor vehicles with highly or fully automated driving functions (Straßenverkehrsgesetz § 1a)
sources.org: Bundesministerium der Justiz / Bundesamt für Justiz
sources.topic: Automated mobility
sources.summary: Section 1a of the German Road Traffic Act sets statutory conditions for operating motor vehicles with highly or fully automated driving functions. It forms part of Germany’s legal allocation of functions between automated driving technology and the human driver and establishes a national operational layer alongside vehicle technical regulation.
sources.why_it_matters: Germany’s StVG is a key comparative model for allocating legal duties between automated-driving functions and human users during real-world operation on public roads.
sources.keywords: automated mobility
sources.citation: Straßenverkehrsgesetz (StVG), § 1a Kraftfahrzeuge mit hoch- oder vollautomatisierter Fahrfunktion.

sources.title: Germany – AFGBV autonomous-vehicle approval and operation
sources.topic: Vehicle permit, operating-area approval and registration for autonomous vehicles
sources.summary: Germany's AFGBV requires an autonomous vehicle to have both a vehicle operating permit and an authority-approved defined operating area before road registration and autonomous operation.
sources.why_it_matters: It provides a concrete legal architecture for turning an ADS technical capability into geographically bounded lawful deployment and is a strong comparator for Slovak operation approval.
sources.keywords: Germany; AFGBV; autonomous vehicle; Level 4; operating permit; Betriebserlaubnis; defined operating area; operating-area approval; registration; insurance; market surveillance; Technische Aufsicht; testing; data storage
sources.citation: Germany, Verordnung zur Genehmigung und zum Betrieb von Kraftfahrzeugen mit autonomer Fahrfunktion in festgelegten Betriebsbereichen (AFGBV), 24 June 2022 (BGBl. I p. 986), effective 1 July 2022, as amended.

sources.title: Germany – autonomous vehicles in defined operating areas (StVG §§ 1d–1g)
sources.topic: Autonomous-vehicle operation in approved defined operating areas
sources.summary: Germany permits Level 4-type autonomous vehicles to operate without an onboard driver only within a legally defined operating area and with a dedicated technical-supervision architecture.
sources.why_it_matters: The German model demonstrates that vehicle technical approval and lawful road operation are separate regulatory gates; the ODD is translated into an authority-approved geographic operating area.
sources.keywords: Germany; StVG; autonomous driving; Level 4; defined operating area; festgelegter Betriebsbereich; Technische Aufsicht; Halter; minimum-risk state; road traffic rules; data recording; liability; remote supervision
sources.citation: Germany, Straßenverkehrsgesetz (StVG), §§ 1d–1g, provisions introduced by Gesetz zum autonomen Fahren of 12 July 2021 (BGBl. I p. 3108), effective 28 July 2021, current consolidated text.

sources.title: Government Bill amending laws in connection with expanding the framework for introducing and using automated vehicles in the Slovak Republic (Parliamentary Print 1329)
sources.org: Government of the Slovak Republic / Ministry of Transport of the Slovak Republic
sources.topic: Expansion of Slovak operational framework for automated vehicles
sources.summary: Slovak Government Bill, Parliamentary Print 1329, proposes a broader framework for automated and fully automated vehicle deployment. It introduces dedicated operator licensing, control-centre and supervision roles, operational documentation, operational-design-domain and minimum-safe-state duties, and recording requirements beyond the existing trial-focused legal framework.
sources.why_it_matters: If enacted, the bill would materially reshape Slovakia’s deployment framework by institutionalising operators, control centres, supervision and operational duties for fully automated vehicles.
sources.keywords: Slovakia; parliamentary print 1329; automated vehicles; fully automated vehicle operator; control centre; supervision operator; licence; operational documentation; ODD; minimum safe state; recording system; deployment
sources.citation: Národná rada Slovenskej republiky, parlamentná tlač 1329, Vládny návrh zákona, ktorým sa menia a dopĺňajú niektoré zákony v súvislosti s rozšírením rámca zavádzania a využívania automatizovaných vozidiel v Slovenskej republike, doručený 7.5.2026.

sources.title: Highways and Locomotives (Amendment) Act 1878
sources.topic: History of mobility regulation – regulatory recalibration before motor-car normalisation
sources.summary: The Highways and Locomotives (Amendment) Act 1878 revised the Victorian statutory framework governing locomotives on highways rather than simply removing earlier restrictions. It demonstrates the incremental adjustment of legal rules as road technology, infrastructure and experience evolved during the nineteenth century.
sources.why_it_matters: The Act prevents an oversimplified narrative of sudden deregulation and shows that regulation of new mobility technologies typically evolves through layered amendments and institutional learning.
sources.keywords: history of mobility regulation; road locomotives; 1878; regulatory recalibration; red flag; horses; local regulation; regulatory learning; automated vehicles
sources.citation: UK Parliament, Highways and Locomotives (Amendment) Act 1878, 41 & 42 Vict. c. 77.

sources.title: China Road Traffic Safety Law revision draft – autonomous vehicles
sources.org: State Council of the People's Republic of China
sources.topic: National road-traffic framework for automated vehicles
sources.summary: China's 2026 Road Traffic Safety Law revision draft adds a dedicated chapter on autonomous vehicles covering ADS activation within design operating conditions, traffic-rule conformity, violations, accident data, insurance and post-market supervision.
sources.why_it_matters: A national road-use framework complements China's technical ADS standards and shifts road-traffic accountability toward the manufacturer/importer when the ADS is active.
sources.keywords: China; Road Traffic Safety Law; autonomous vehicles; automated driving; Articles 95-103; dynamic driving task; design operating conditions; ODD; manufacturer; importer; traffic violations; burden of proof; accident data; insurance; data governance; post-market supervision; driver assistance; functional unmanned vehicles
sources.citation: Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, 中华人民共和国道路交通安全法（修订草案）, first reviewed 25 August 2026; public consultation opened 28 August 2026 and closes 26 September 2026.

sources.title: Locomotive Act 1861
sources.topic: History of mobility regulation – early road-locomotive regulation
sources.summary: The Locomotive Act 1861 regulated the use of mechanically propelled locomotives on British roads, including speed and operating restrictions and mechanisms for local controls. It represents an early legislative response to a disruptive road technology before the emergence of the modern motor-vehicle regulatory system.
sources.why_it_matters: The Act provides a historical comparator for how law initially responds to unfamiliar vehicle technology through restrictive operating conditions before broader regulatory normalisation develops.
sources.keywords: history of mobility regulation; regulatory normalisation; road locomotives; traction engines; speed limits; banning orders; technological change; automated vehicles
sources.citation: UK Parliament, Locomotive Act 1861, 24 & 25 Vict. c. 70.

sources.title: Locomotives Act 1865 (Red Flag Act)
sources.topic: History of mobility regulation – exceptional regulation of novel road technology
sources.summary: The Locomotives Act 1865 tightened restrictions on road locomotives, including lower speed limits and the well-known requirement for a person to precede certain locomotives carrying a red flag. It illustrates a precautionary regulatory response to perceived safety and nuisance risks from emerging road technology.
sources.why_it_matters: The Act is a classic example of restrictive technology regulation and helps frame debates about proportionality, safety evidence and the risk of over-regulating automated vehicles.
sources.keywords: history of mobility regulation; Red Flag Act; locomotives; road safety; speed limits; flagman; precaution; regulatory normalisation; automated vehicles
sources.citation: UK Parliament, Locomotives Act 1865, 28 & 29 Vict. c. 83.

sources.title: Locomotives on Highways Act 1896
sources.topic: History of mobility regulation – legal reclassification and controlled liberalisation of motor vehicles
sources.summary: The Locomotives on Highways Act 1896 liberalised aspects of the British legal framework for light locomotives and is commonly associated with the end of the most restrictive red-flag requirements. It marked a significant stage in the transition toward a regulatory regime better suited to motor vehicles.
sources.why_it_matters: The Act illustrates regulatory normalisation: rules initially designed for an unfamiliar technology were recalibrated as technical capability and societal experience developed.
sources.keywords: history of mobility regulation; light locomotive; deemed carriage; legal fiction; regulatory bridge; delegated regulation; motor vehicles; regulatory normalisation
sources.citation: UK Parliament, Locomotives on Highways Act 1896, 59 & 60 Vict. c. 36.

sources.title: Motor Car Act 1903
sources.topic: History of mobility regulation – registration, driver licensing and motor-car governance
sources.summary: The Motor Car Act 1903 developed the United Kingdom’s early motor-vehicle regulatory framework, including vehicle registration, driver licensing and speed regulation. It represents the shift from exceptional treatment of mechanically propelled vehicles toward durable institutions and legal categories for ordinary motor traffic.
sources.why_it_matters: The Act shows how regulation can move from technology-specific restrictions toward licensing, registration and behavioural rules, a useful historical comparison for automated-vehicle deployment.
sources.keywords: history of mobility regulation; Motor Car Act 1903; vehicle registration; driver licensing; speed; enforcement; making the driver; regulatory normalisation
sources.citation: UK Parliament, Motor Car Act 1903, 3 Edw. 7 c. 36.

sources.title: Ordonnance No. 2021-443 of 14 April 2021 on criminal liability and conditions of use for vehicles with delegated driving (Ordonnance n° 2021-443)
sources.topic: France - legal basis for automated driving and automated road transport systems
sources.summary: French Ordonnance No. 2021-443 establishes rules on criminal liability and conditions of use for vehicles with delegated driving. It created key provisions in the French Road Code and forms a central part of France’s legal framework for allocating responsibility and regulating automated-driving use on public roads.
sources.why_it_matters: The Ordonnance provides a mature national model for assigning legal responsibility and operational conditions when automated driving is used in ordinary road traffic.
sources.keywords: France; automated driving; delegated driving; automated road transport system; criminal liability; remote intervention; service organiser; operator; safety; deployment
sources.citation: France, Ordonnance 2021-443 du 14 avril 2021, Journal officiel, 15 April 2021.

sources.title: Road Traffic Act 1930
sources.topic: History of mobility regulation – system-level regulation of automobility
sources.summary: The Road Traffic Act 1930 consolidated and modernised major parts of British road-traffic regulation and repealed earlier statutes including the Locomotives on Highways Act 1896 and Motor Car Act 1903. It reflects the maturation of motor-vehicle regulation into a more comprehensive road-traffic framework.
sources.why_it_matters: The Act demonstrates institutional consolidation after technological adoption and provides a historical model for how fragmented rules can evolve into a comprehensive mobility regulatory framework.
sources.keywords: history of mobility regulation; Road Traffic Act 1930; driver; vehicle construction; dangerous driving; compulsory insurance; liability; system of automobility
sources.citation: UK Parliament, Road Traffic Act 1930, 20 & 21 Geo. 5 c. 43.

sources.title: The Automated Vehicles (Permits for Automated Passenger Services) Regulations 2026
sources.topic: Automated passenger services – staged operational permitting
sources.summary: UK Statutory Instrument 2026 No. 439 establishes detailed procedures for permits for automated passenger services under the Automated Vehicles Act 2024. It regulates grant, variation, suspension and withdrawal of permits and supports automated buses in Great Britain and automated taxi-like services in England.
sources.why_it_matters: The Regulations operationalise a service-level deployment pathway for automated passenger transport and illustrate regulation beyond vehicle approval, including permits for real-world commercial operation.
sources.keywords: Automated Vehicles Act 2024; automated passenger services; permit; deployment; trials; commercial service; variation; suspension; withdrawal; staged implementation; legal bridge
sources.citation: The Automated Vehicles (Permits for Automated Passenger Services) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/439.

sources.title: Locomotives on Highways Bill – House of Commons debate, 30 June 1896
sources.topic: History of mobility regulation – parliamentary debate on motor-vehicle liberalisation and adaptive regulation
sources.summary: House of Commons debate on the Locomotives on Highways Bill shortly before enactment of the 1896 statute. The parliamentary discussion records contemporary arguments about road safety, technological development and the suitability of existing restrictions for newer mechanically propelled vehicles.
sources.why_it_matters: The debate provides primary evidence of how legislators balanced innovation and road safety when replacing earlier restrictions, a useful historical analogue for automated-vehicle regulation.
sources.keywords: history of mobility regulation; Hansard; 1896; innovation; safety; competitiveness; elastic regulation; infrastructure adaptation; locomotives; motor vehicles
sources.citation: UK Parliament, HC Deb 30 June 1896, ‘Locomotives on Highways Bill’.

sources.title: Royal Commission on Motor Cars – House of Lords debate, 13 March 1906
sources.topic: History of mobility regulation – ex-post regulatory learning after early motor-car legislation
sources.summary: House of Lords debate concerning the Royal Commission on Motor Cars and the regulatory problems created by growing motor traffic. The discussion captures contemporary concerns about safety, enforcement and the adaptation of road law after motor vehicles had moved beyond the earliest experimental stage.
sources.why_it_matters: The debate illustrates how governance questions persist after initial legalisation and supports comparison with the institutional and enforcement challenges that may follow automated-vehicle deployment.
sources.keywords: history of mobility regulation; Royal Commission; 1906; motor cars; bad driving; road dust; speed limits; regulatory learning; anticipatory governance
sources.citation: UK Parliament, HL Deb 13 March 1906, vol. 153, cc. 1063–1066, ‘Royal Commission on Motor Cars’.

sources.title: Automated Vehicles Act implementation programme
sources.org: Centre for Connected and Autonomous Vehicles
sources.topic: Automated Vehicles Act 2024 – staged implementation to 2027
sources.summary: Official UK government programme coordinating policy, legislation and operational work needed to implement the Automated Vehicles Act 2024. It supports safe deployment, trialling and development of automated-vehicle use cases and sets out the institutional programme leading toward full implementation of the statutory regime.
sources.why_it_matters: The programme shows how the UK is sequencing secondary legislation, trialling and institutional preparation to move from an enacted framework toward operational deployment of automated vehicles.
sources.keywords: Automated Vehicles Act 2024; implementation; authorisation; in-use regulation; automated passenger services; trials; 2027; staged deployment; regulatory normalisation
sources.citation: Department for Transport and Centre for Connected and Autonomous Vehicles, ‘Automated Vehicles Act implementation programme’ (GOV.UK, 2025, current 2026 implementation page).

sources.title: Automated vehicles: statement of safety principles consultation
sources.org: UK Department for Transport; Centre for Connected and Autonomous Vehicles
sources.topic: Automated Vehicles Act 2024 – statement of safety principles
sources.summary: Official UK consultation on the draft statutory statement of safety principles for self-driving vehicles in Great Britain. The draft sets ten behaviour-based principles intended to inform authorisation and subsequent monitoring under the Automated Vehicles Act 2024, including compliance with the authorised domain and adaptation to the territory of operation.
sources.why_it_matters: The consultation develops the statutory safety benchmark that will guide authorisation of self-driving vehicles in Great Britain and is therefore central to the UK deployment regime.

sources.citation: UK Department for Transport and Centre for Connected and Autonomous Vehicles, Automated vehicles: statement of safety principles consultation, 17 June 2026, CP 1598.

sources.topic: Annual AV disengagement and testing-mileage reporting
sources.summary: Official California DMV reporting for the December 2024 to November 2025 testing period documents autonomous-vehicle testing mileage and disengagement information submitted by permit holders. The DMV reported more than nine million autonomous test miles and provides access to the annual reports used to assess testing exposure and safety-driver interventions.
sources.why_it_matters: These reports provide real-world regulatory evidence on testing exposure and human interventions, useful for comparing state oversight metrics with EU and UNECE safety-assurance approaches.

sources.title: China's first conditional L3 vehicle approvals and road-access pilots
sources.org: Ministry of Industry and Information Technology
sources.topic: Conditional L3 product admission linked to geographically limited public-road operation
sources.summary: MIIT conditionally approved two L3 automated-driving vehicle models in December 2025, limiting ADS activation to specified Beijing and Chongqing road segments, speed ceilings and designated operating entities.
sources.why_it_matters: The decision shows a staged deployment model in which technical product admission is combined with a separate, geographically limited road-use pilot rather than unrestricted market access.

sources.topic: Croatian legal model for fully automated passenger transport and real-world service testing
sources.summary: Právna analýza chorvátskeho modelu povoľovania a testovania plne automatizovanej osobnej dopravy. Ukazuje, že národný test funguje ako pred-deploymentová validácia konkrétnej služby a lokálneho nasadenia nad rámec európskeho typového schvaľovania ADS.
sources.why_it_matters: Ide o detailný európsky príklad service-level assurance pre robotaxi: prepája licenciu, reálne podmienky, územie, remote operations, incidenty, údržbu a kybernetickú bezpečnosť a zároveň presne pomenúva otvorený problém retestingu pri prechode na driverless prevádzku.

sources.org: Working Group “Research Needs in Teleoperation”; coordination: Tom Michael Gasser; Alexander Frey
sources.topic: Research and regulatory requirements for remote assistance and remote driving
sources.summary: An official BASt working-group report sets out a comprehensive research agenda for remote assistance and remote driving, covering functional safety, control centres, communications, teleoperator workstations, competence requirements, acceptance and road safety.
sources.why_it_matters: It supplies a rigorous conceptual distinction between assistance and direct remote control and demonstrates that safe teleoperation requires coordinated regulation of technology, communications, human performance, organisational responsibilities and the permitted operational area.

sources.title: Regulating the new – technology regulation, ethics and legitimacy
sources.topic: Technology regulation and sociotechnical governance
sources.summary: Open-access 2026 textbook offering a systematic method for regulators to assess emerging technologies, identify ethical and legal gaps, justify intervention and choose regulatory instruments.
sources.why_it_matters: Provides a regulator-facing, multidisciplinary methodology that can serve as a conceptual scaffold for ROAT analysis and teaching on automated-transport governance.

sources.title: Steam engines on UK roads, 1862–1865: Banning orders, agricultural locomotives and the ‘red flag’ Act
sources.topic: History of mobility regulation – precaution, nuisance and early road-locomotive law
sources.summary: John Agnew’s peer-reviewed historical study examines British regulation of steam road locomotives between 1862 and 1865, including local banning orders, agricultural locomotives and the emergence of the red-flag requirement. It reconstructs the policy and legislative context surrounding early attempts to govern mechanically propelled road vehicles.
sources.why_it_matters: The article provides historical evidence for analysing how safety concerns, public acceptance and restrictive operating rules shape the early regulatory phase of disruptive road technologies.
sources.keywords: steam engines; road locomotives; banning orders; agricultural locomotives; Red Flag Act; precaution; nuisance; technological progress; legal history
sources.citation: John Agnew, ‘Steam engines on UK roads, 1862–1865: Banning orders, agricultural locomotives and the ‘red flag’ Act’, 90 The International Journal for the History of Engineering & Technology 53–74 (2020), DOI 10.1080/17581206.2020.1797447.

sources.title: The Development of Traffic Liability
sources.topic: Comparative legal history – traffic liability, technological risk and insurance
sources.summary: Edited by Wolfgang Ernst, this comparative legal-history volume examines the development of traffic liability across several Western European jurisdictions. It analyses how legal systems responded to road and railway accident risks through differing combinations of fault liability, strict liability, insurance, statutory regulation and other institutional mechanisms.
sources.why_it_matters: The book offers comparative historical evidence on how mobility-related liability regimes normalise differently across jurisdictions, providing context for future automated-vehicle liability models.
sources.keywords: traffic liability; legal history; motor vehicles; railways; technological risk; fault; strict liability; no-fault liability; insurance; comparative law; England; France; Germany; Netherlands; Spain; Sweden
sources.citation: Wolfgang Ernst (ed.), The Development of Traffic Liability (Cambridge University Press 2010), ISBN 978-0-521-19208-8.

sources.title: Tort Law, Risk, and Technological Innovation in England
sources.topic: History of mobility regulation – tort, insurance and socialisation of technological risk
sources.summary: Ken Oliphant’s peer-reviewed article examines how technological innovation and associated risks influenced the development of English tort law from the Industrial Revolution onward. It considers the interaction between tort liability and alternative mechanisms including insurance, regulation and social welfare in responding to new technological harms.
sources.why_it_matters: The article provides a legal-history framework for evaluating how liability adapts to technological risk and helps contextualise contemporary debates about automated-vehicle responsibility and compensation.
sources.keywords: tort law; technological innovation; motor vehicles; risk; liability; insurance; loss spreading; legal history; regulatory normalisation
sources.citation: Ken Oliphant, ‘Tort Law, Risk, and Technological Innovation in England’, 59 McGill Law Journal 819 (2014).

sources.title: GB 44721-2026 – Safety Requirements for Autonomous Driving Systems
sources.org: Ministry of Industry and Information Technology; State Administration for Market Regulation; Standardization Administration of China
sources.topic: Mandatory national safety standard for L3/L4 automated-driving systems
sources.summary: China's new mandatory national safety standard applies to L3 and L4 automated-driving systems on M- and N-category vehicles and is scheduled to take effect on 1 July 2027.
sources.why_it_matters: It creates the technical safety pillar for China's move from automated-driving pilots toward scaled product approval and complements the proposed national road-traffic rules.

sources.citation: GB 44721—2026, 智能网联汽车 自动驾驶系统安全要求 [Safety Requirements for Autonomous Driving Systems], issued 30 July 2026 by SAMR/SAC under MIIT standardisation work; effective 1 July 2027.

sources.title: SAE J3016_202104 – Taxonomy and Definitions for Terms Related to Driving Automation Systems for On-Road Motor Vehicles
sources.topic: Technical standards
sources.summary: SAE J3016 provides a widely used taxonomy and definitions for driving automation systems, including the levels of driving automation and concepts such as the dynamic driving task, operational design domain, fallback and roles of human users. The April 2021 revision remains an important terminology reference across technical and regulatory work.
sources.why_it_matters: The standard supplies the terminology used to distinguish ADS functions and human roles, supporting consistent comparison of national, EU, UNECE and industry automated-driving frameworks.
sources.keywords: Technical standards; Safety; automated vehicles
sources.citation: SAE International, SAE J3016_202104, Taxonomy and Definitions for Terms Related to Driving Automation Systems for On-Road Motor Vehicles, revised 30 April 2021.

sources.title: Historical background of the Conventions related to road traffic and traffic safety
sources.topic: History of international road-traffic conventions and separation of vehicle-construction and road-use regulation
sources.summary: UNECE document ECE/TRANS/WP.1/GE.3/2022/7 reviews the historical development of international conventions concerning road traffic and traffic safety. It traces the evolution of legal instruments that preceded and shaped contemporary international road-traffic governance, including the progression toward the Geneva and Vienna conventions.
sources.why_it_matters: The report provides an authoritative historical bridge for assessing how international traffic law adapts over time and contextualises present efforts to accommodate automated driving.

sources.citation: UNECE, Historical background of the Conventions related to road traffic and traffic safety, ECE/TRANS/WP.1/GE.3/2022/7, 22 June 2022.

sources.summary: Official UNECE working document containing the proposal for a new UN Regulation on Automated Driving Systems considered by WP.29 at its 199th session in June 2026. sources.why_it_matters: The document is important for understanding how regulators may interpret and apply the new UNECE ADS instruments consistently after their adoption.

sources.title: UNECE proposal aligns remote intervention and remote interaction
sources.topic: Interpretation of remote intervention and remote interaction in the ADS Guidance and Interpretation Document
sources.summary: ADS-21-71/Rev.2 proposes treating remote intervention and remote interaction as equivalent situations in which external support addresses tactical functions while the ADS continues to perform the entire dynamic driving task.
sources.why_it_matters: The document is a rare cross-framework comparison linking UNECE terminology with SAE J3016, EU Regulation 2022/1426, AVSC guidance and the forthcoming ISO/PAS 26361. Its deferred status also shows that the terminology remains unsettled.
